candidates.title: The state of research on leader humor
candidates.why_it_adds_value: Fills the humor single-source gap with an independent systematic review plus meta-analysis and path analyses of leader humor. It separates being a funny person (trait humor) from actually using humor (humor expression), and openly lists problems with construct clarity, measurement and theory, which gives the library a sober counterweight to Humor, Seriously, whose authors have an incentive to stress benefits.
candidates.credibility: Peer-reviewed in Organizational Psychology Review (SAGE, vol. 9, no. 1, pp. 3 to 40). Cooper is a leading leader-humor researcher (University of Miami); Sosik is a Penn State leadership scholar; Kong publishes in top management journals. Over 100 Scopus citations per the Penn State portal.
candidates.evidence_quality: High for a balanced picture of what is and is not known: systematic review with a quantitative synthesis. The underlying studies are mostly correlational field surveys, so causal claims about humor making leaders effective remain weak, which the authors themselves flag.
key_ideas_preview: Being seen as a humorous person and actually using humor at work are different things and should be measured and taught separately.
Leader humor is linked to better follower attitudes, but most evidence is correlational and cannot show that humor causes those outcomes.
The field still lacks agreed definitions and measures, so confident percentage claims about humor at work deserve skepticism.
Several theoretical lenses (relational, affective, social exchange) explain why humor might help, and they predict different boundary conditions.
candidates.overlap_with_core_books: Partial overlap with Humor, Seriously on leader humor benefits; independent authorship. Cooper's related work (Cooper, Kong and Crossley, 2018) is not a core book source as far as Stage 1 records show.
candidates.access: Journal article (SAGE); abstract on Penn State and University of Colorado research portals; full text via library.

candidates.title: A meta-analysis of positive humor in the workplace
candidates.why_it_adds_value: The standard independent quantitative summary of humor at work (49 samples, about 8,500 people), covering both employee and supervisor humor. It gives the library a research anchor for humor insights that currently rest on one book, and it carries its own caution: positive, self-directed coping humor looks safe to encourage, while promoting humor broadly can backfire (derogatory humor, legal risk).
candidates.credibility: Peer-reviewed in Journal of Managerial Psychology 27(2), 155 to 190. Viswesvaran is a highly cited meta-analysis methodologist in industrial-organizational psychology (Florida International University).
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. Proper meta-analysis, but of correlational studies, so it shows associations (with cohesion, coping, performance, lower burnout and withdrawal) rather than causation; effects are modest; negative humor was understudied at the time; now over a decade old.
key_ideas_preview: Positive humor at work goes with better coping, team cohesion and performance, and with less burnout, stress and withdrawal.
Supervisor humor is tied to more satisfied subordinates and more cohesive teams.
These are associations of modest size; they do not show that adding jokes will improve results.
Encouraging people to use humor to cope with stress is lower risk than encouraging humor aimed at others.
candidates.overlap_with_core_books: Same broad claim as Humor, Seriously (humor helps at work) but independent and more cautious; useful to temper the book's stronger causal language.
candidates.access: Journal article (Emerald); abstract and secondary summaries open; full text via library.

candidates.title: The Extended Transportation-Imagery Model: A Meta-Analysis of the Antecedents and Consequences of Consumers' Narrative Transportation
candidates.why_it_adds_value: Provides the narrative transportation research base the storytelling subcategory lacks beyond Made to Stick. It synthesizes two decades of work (132 effect sizes from 76 articles) on what makes listeners mentally enter a story and how that shifts their attitudes and intentions, giving research-backed story ingredients to replace or check the unconfirmed story spine.
candidates.credibility: Peer-reviewed in Journal of Consumer Research 40(5), 797 to 817, a top marketing journal. Builds on Green and Brock's transportation theory. Authors are established narrative and consumer researchers.
candidates.evidence_quality: High for the existence of transportation effects and their main drivers; quantitative synthesis across many studies, including unpublished ones. Limitation: many studies use advertising and consumer stimuli, so transfer to workplace stories is an inference.
key_ideas_preview: Stories persuade largely by transporting the listener: absorbing them so they stop counter-arguing.
Identifiable characters, an imaginable plot and a sense of realism make transportation more likely.
Transportation shifts beliefs, attitudes and intentions, and lowers critical thinking about the message.
Listener factors matter too: attention and familiarity with the story world increase transportation.
candidates.overlap_with_core_books: Complements Made to Stick's Stories principle and its simulation idea with a measured mechanism; little direct overlap in content.
candidates.access: Open-access accepted manuscript on City Research Online (City, University of London); journal version via library.

candidates.title: Meta-analytic evidence for the persuasive effect of narratives on beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors
candidates.why_it_adds_value: Gives an honest size estimate for storytelling's persuasive power across beliefs, attitudes, intentions and behaviors. It reports a reliable but small effect, which corrects inflated claims such as the 63 percent versus 5 percent stories-versus-statistics figure flagged in Stage 2, and so helps calibrate how much to promise about stories.
candidates.credibility: Peer-reviewed in Communication Monographs 83(4), 446 to 467, a flagship communication journal. Dillard is a leading persuasion scholar (Penn State); Braddock researches narrative persuasion.
candidates.evidence_quality: High for the overall conclusion (narratives persuade, modestly). Effects are small (correlations around 0.2 per secondary summaries) and heterogeneous with unexplained moderators; secondary sources report weaker results for some story types, which should be checked against the full text before being cited.
key_ideas_preview: Stories do change minds and behavior, but the average effect is small, not dramatic.
Narrative effects appear across beliefs, attitudes, intentions and actual behavior.
Results vary a lot between studies, so a story is a useful tool rather than a guaranteed winner over data.
Pairing a story with clear evidence is a safer bet than relying on either alone (inference from the small, variable effects).
candidates.overlap_with_core_books: Tests the core claim behind Made to Stick's Stories chapter; independent of the book.
candidates.access: Journal article (Taylor and Francis); abstract open; full text via library.

candidates.title: The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think?
candidates.why_it_adds_value: Directly about first meetings with new people, which the introductions subcategory lacks. Five studies show that after meeting someone, people underestimate how much the other person liked them, in the lab, among new dorm mates for months, and in a workshop, and that self-critical rumination drives it. This gives a research-based reason to follow up after an introduction instead of assuming it went badly.
candidates.credibility: Peer-reviewed in Psychological Science 29(11), 1742 to 1756. Clark (Yale) is a senior relationships researcher; Sandstrom (Essex, now Sussex) leads research on talking to strangers. Data posted on the Open Science Framework.
candidates.evidence_quality: High. Multiple studies with different samples and settings, open data, and later extensions by other teams. Effect concerns perceptions, not behavior change from an intervention.
key_ideas_preview: After meeting someone new, people consistently believe they were liked less than they actually were.
The gap comes from replaying your own awkward moments, which hides the other person's signs of liking.
The gap can last for months among new acquaintances, so do not let it stop you from following up.
Even outside observers see more liking than the self-critical participant does.
candidates.overlap_with_core_books: Fits the miscalibration cluster (Stage 2, section 2.4) and may be mentioned in passing in Talk or How to Know a Person, but it is not a tagged core insight and comes from a different lab than the Epley papers, adding independence.
candidates.access: Open-access record on the University of Essex repository; journal via SAGE.

candidates.title: The Surprise of Reaching Out: Appreciated More Than We Think
candidates.why_it_adds_value: Covers the follow-up and reconnecting part of the introductions and networking gap. Across 13 experiments with over 5,900 participants, people who reach out underestimate how much the recipient appreciates it, especially when the contact is a surprise or goes to a weak tie, which is exactly the post-introduction follow-up people hesitate over.
candidates.credibility: Peer-reviewed in Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 124(4), 754 to 771 (online 2022), a top social psychology journal; Liu is a marketing and psychology researcher at the University of Pittsburgh. Covered by an APA press release.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium to High. Large multi-experiment package with a consistent effect and a tested mechanism (surprise). Relies on self-reported appreciation and short-term outcomes; single team so far.
key_ideas_preview: People underestimate how much a quick check-in or follow-up message is appreciated.
The more surprising the contact, the bigger the underestimate, because recipients enjoy the surprise.
The gap is larger for weak ties, such as someone you were recently introduced to.
A short, unprompted message is enough; it does not need a reason or a gift.
candidates.overlap_with_core_books: Same family as the Epley-style miscalibration findings in Talk and How to Know a Person, but from an independent team and applied to follow-up, which no core insight covers.
candidates.access: APA journal via library; press release and university summaries open.

candidates.title: Overcoming the Self-Promotion Dilemma: Interpersonal Attraction and Extra Help as a Consequence of Who Sings One's Praises
candidates.why_it_adds_value: The only research candidate found that speaks to introducing others and being introduced. Three experiments show that having someone else describe your accomplishments makes you more liked and more likely to get help than praising yourself, even when the introducer has an interest in promoting you. It supports a practical introductions playbook: introduce others generously, and let others introduce you.
candidates.credibility: Peer-reviewed in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 32(10), 1362 to 1374. Pfeffer (Stanford GSB) and Cialdini (Arizona State) are among the most cited scholars in organizational behavior and persuasion.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. Three experiments with consistent results, but small lab samples with students and no large replication located; context is hiring and evaluation rather than social introductions.
key_ideas_preview: Self-promotion carries a likability cost; the same praise from a third party does not.
An introducer with a stake in you still helps, so a colleague's warm introduction is worth asking for.
When you introduce two people, naming each person's strengths does them a favor they cannot do for themselves.
Being introduced well makes others more willing to help, not just more impressed.
candidates.overlap_with_core_books: None found; core books do not address third-party introductions.
candidates.access: Journal article (SAGE) via library; Stanford GSB faculty page and 2006 Stanford Insights summary open.

candidates.title: Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
candidates.why_it_adds_value: Adds a quantitative research base to group dynamics. Pooling 22 studies (5,279 people in 1,356 groups), it finds a general group ability factor that depends more on how members collaborate than on individual skill, and that it rises with members' social perceptiveness. This grounds advice about who speaks, how turns are shared, and reading the room, beyond Supercommunicators' reliance on one group study.
candidates.credibility: Peer-reviewed in PNAS 118(21). Woolley (Carnegie Mellon) and Malone (MIT Center for Collective Intelligence) originated the collective intelligence construct.
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium to High. Large pooled dataset and a direct answer to earlier critiques of the original 2010 Science paper, which some researchers had questioned; but it comes from the originating team, so it is not fully independent, and links to specific conversational behaviors are partly inferred.
key_ideas_preview: Groups have a measurable general ability to work together that carries across different tasks.
How a group collaborates predicts its performance more than how skilled its individual members are.
Groups whose members read others' emotions and intentions well perform better.
Improving group process, such as coordination and participation, is a practical lever for better results.
candidates.overlap_with_core_books: Supercommunicators touches group conversation through Sievers et al.; this is a separate, broader evidence base. No core book cites it as far as Stage 1 records show.
candidates.access: Open access in PubMed Central and MIT DSpace.

notes: Ranked priorities: humor (Kong et al. 2019; Mesmer-Magnus et al. 2012) gives two independent research reviews to balance Humor, Seriously; both stress that the evidence is mostly correlational. Storytelling gains a mechanism (van Laer et al. 2014 on transportation) and a size check (Braddock and Dillard 2016: real but small effects). Introductions gain three papers on first meetings, being introduced and following up; no well-evidenced practitioner book on introductions was found (popular networking books such as Never Eat Alone are anecdotal). Verified alternates not included to stay within eight: Frazier, Fainshmidt, Klinger, Pezeshkan and Vracheva (2017), 'Psychological Safety: A Meta-Analytic Review and Extension', Personnel Psychology 70(1), 113 to 165, 136 samples, open access at Old Dominion University (strong second group-dynamics source; overlaps with meetings and could go to the professional agent); and Levin, Walter and Murnighan (2011), 'Dormant Ties: The Value of Reconnecting', Organization Science 22(4), 923 to 939 (reconnecting with old contacts gives both novelty and trust; fits relationships/networking). Some details for Braddock and Dillard and Mesmer-Magnus come from abstracts and secondary summaries and should be checked against full text before citing exact numbers. Several publisher pages (PMC, APA, City) returned blocked or empty responses to curl; their details were checked through bibliographic records (RePEc, university repositories).
